diagnostic_evidence.quote: The average $\sigma_j(B)$s should then correspond to bounds for the $k$ quantiles of the eigenvalues of $A$ as in \eqref{eq:interlacing}.
In particular, after fixing $k$, our framework provides bounds in expectation on the $k$ spectrum quantiles of the kernel matrix $A$.

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that the framework yields (expectation-level) bounds on the eigenvalue quantiles of A without forming A. What the formal content can at best establish is: (i) a pointwise interlacing criterion that presupposes exact equality of the first k power traces of the given matrices A and B (Corollary cor:momentmatching), and (ii) closeness of EXPECTED traces for the randomized construction (Proposition prop:momentmatch). Nothing in the paper connects expectation-level moment matching, nor the m-trial averaging of sigma_j(B), to bounds on the eigenvalues of the realized matrix A; that concentration/transfer step is only asserted ('should then correspond'). The guarantee type advertised (bounds on the eigenvalues themselves) is therefore not established even if the formal results were repaired.

failure_location.quote: This framework gives meaningful bounds for all the eigenvalues of a kernel matrix while avoiding the cost of constructing the full matrix.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Weaken the advertised claims to what is proven (approximate matching of expected normalized power traces, plus empirical quantile accuracy), or supply a genuine concentration argument transferring expectation-level moment matching to bounds for the realized eigenvalues of A.
issues.overall_effect: The headline guarantee (a priori, subquadratic quantile bounds for all eigenvalues) is unsupported; only expected-trace matching plus empirical evidence exist, and the abstract, Section 1, Section 3 and the conclusion all state the stronger, unproven guarantee.
issues.title: Advertised eigenvalue-quantile bound guarantee exceeds what is proven
issues.why_classification: A limited weakening of the advertised claims leaves a recognizably comparable contribution (the randomized moment-matching method with expected-trace guarantees and empirical evidence), so no new proof architecture is forced; but the repair withdraws a stated guarantee, so it is more than minor.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: we set $B=\kappa(Y,Y)$ and find its eigenvalues
which we may compute in $O(k^2)$ time \cite{golubvanloan}
In particular, it requires $O(mk^2)$ steps, where $m$ is the number of times we form $B$.

issues.failure_explanation: Each of the m trials must form B and then compute its eigenvalues ('we set B=kappa(Y,Y) and find its eigenvalues'). Forming B costs O(k^2) kernel evaluations, but computing all eigenvalues of a general k x k symmetric matrix costs Theta(k^3) arithmetic operations (Golub-Van Loan, the cited reference). The advertised totals 'O(mk^2) computations' and 'we may compute [the k eigenvalues of B] in O(k^2) time' are therefore false; only the subquadratic-in-n claim survives, since k is fixed independently of n.

failure_location.quote: This new framework requires $O(mk^2)$ computations, where $m$ is a constant that depends on the desired approximation accuracy.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the cost as O(mk^2) kernel evaluations plus O(mk^3) for the m eigendecompositions (i.e., O(mk^3) total); the subquadratic-in-n claim survives unchanged.
issues.overall_effect: The stated complexity guarantee (in the introduction, Section 2 and the conclusion) understates the cost by a factor of k; the subquadratic-in-n selling point is not affected.
issues.title: Advertised O(mk^2) complexity omits the O(k^3) eigendecompositions
issues.why_classification: A local rewording of the operation count preserves every substantive guarantee, including subquadratic running time in n.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Denote by $a_i$ and $b_j$ the $i$th and $j$th largest elements of $S$ and $T$, respectively
where we define $b_0=0$ and $b_{k+1}=\infty$
Then $\sigma_{\lceil\frac{jk}{n}\rceil-1}(B)\geq\sigma_j(A)\geq\sigma_{\lceil\frac{jk}{n}\rceil+1}(B)$ for $1\leq j\leq n$, where we define ``$\sigma_0(B)=\infty$'' and ``$\sigma_{k+1}(B)=0$.''

issues.failure_explanation: The proposition orders S and T by decreasing size ('the ith and jth largest elements') and sets b_0 = 0, b_{k+1} = infinity, yet asserts b_{ceil(jk/n)-1} <= a_j <= b_{ceil(jk/n)+1}. Taken literally this says, for j in the first block, max S <= b_2 and, in the last block, b_{k-1} <= min S, which is false: with S = {4,3,2,1} (n=4) and T = {(5+sqrt5)/2, (5-sqrt5)/2} (k=2), the first two power means match (2.5 and 7.5), yet the claim gives 0 <= 4 <= 1.382. The statement as written is the opposite of what its own proof establishes (the CDF bounds F_S(b_i) in [(i-1)/k, i/k] for increasingly ordered roots), of the conventions in Corollary cor:momentmatching (sigma_0(B)=infty, sigma_{k+1}(B)=0), and of Figure fig:momentinterlace.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Order the elements of S and T increasingly (or equivalently flip the two inequalities and interchange the conventions b_0 = infinity, b_{k+1} = 0); the proof, the figure, and Corollary cor:momentmatching then agree with the statement.
issues.overall_effect: The central interlacing proposition asserts false inequalities as written, and the corollary that transfers it to kernel matrices is derived from the reversed version, leaving eq:interlacing without a valid supporting statement.
issues.title: Interlacing inequalities in prop:momentmatching are reversed
issues.why_classification: A local, forced re-convention of the ordering restores full agreement with the proof, the figure, and the corollary; no substantive claim or guarantee is lost.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: and suppose $\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{a_i^r}{n}=\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{b_i^r}{k}$ for all $r=1,\ldots,k$
Since $\nu_i=\mu_i$ for all $i$ and because $T$ has the discrete uniform distribution, this is equivalent to
\sum_{l=1}^k(P_iP_j)(b_l)&=k\delta_{i,j}

issues.failure_explanation: The hypothesis prescribes only the first k power means; equality of the first k moments of an n-point uniform distribution does not determine its higher moments (for S={4,3,2,1}, T as above, the fourth power means are 88.5 vs 87.5). The proof nevertheless requires mu_i = nu_i through order 2k: the Kronecker relation sum_l (P_iP_j)(b_l) = k*delta_ij is derived by replacing the moments of S (up to degree deg(P_i)+deg(P_j) <= 2k) by those of T, and the Christoffel evaluation sum_i P_i(b_j)^2 = k needs moments through order 2k as well. Hence the identification of the b_i with the roots of P_k, the identity C = A^T A = kI, and the final interlacing conclusion are all unestablished under the stated hypothesis; the argument proves nothing under the hypotheses given.

failure_location.quote: our assumptions are equivalent to requiring that $\mu_i=\nu_i$ for each $i=1,\ldots,k$, and therefore for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must either prove the block-interlacing from the stated k-fold moment matching by a new argument, or strengthen the hypothesis to matching through order 2k - which the framework cannot certify, since its moment conditions (eq:specialdistrib, Corollary cor:momentmatching) only reach order k and binom(k, |C|+1) vanishes beyond |C| = k-1.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised 'very general interlacing-type theorem' and, through it, Corollary cor:momentmatching and the whole quantile-bound framework of eq:interlacing lose their only justification.
issues.title: Proof of prop:momentmatching invalidly upgrades k-fold moment matching to all moments
issues.why_classification: The linchpin result is unsupported and the natural in-source repair (matching 2k moments) is structurally unavailable to the framework, so every resolution needs essentially new proof architecture or loses the advertised guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Let $S,T\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}$ with $|S|=n$, $|T|=k$, and $k|n$.
apply Proposition~\ref{prop:momentmatching} while setting $S=\mathcal{A}$ and $T=\mathcal{B}$

issues.failure_explanation: The proof invokes Proposition prop:momentmatching, whose hypothesis requires k | n, but the corollary's statement imposes no divisibility condition; for pairs (A,B) with k not dividing n the cited result simply does not apply, so the stated conclusion is unsupported outside k | n.

failure_location.quote: Suppose $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ and $B\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}$ have distinct, nonnegative eigenvalues, and suppose we have $\mathrm{tr}\left(B^r/k\right)=\mathrm{tr}\left(A^r/n\right)$ for $1\leq r\leq k$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis k | n to the corollary's statement.
issues.overall_effect: The corollary is stated in a strictly larger parameter regime than anything proved; within the paper's framework (which always assumes k | n) the intended use is unaffected.
issues.title: cor:momentmatching omits the divisibility hypothesis k | n required by its proof
issues.why_classification: Adding one standard hypothesis that every application in the paper satisfies restores the result with no loss of content or guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: for all $s\in[t,1]$

\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\frac{\int_{[0,s]^l}e^{-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^r(x_{\pi(i-1)},x_{\pi(i)})^2d\mathbf{x_{S_\pi}}}}{\int_{[0,1]^l}e^{-\lambda\sum_{i=1}^r(x_{\pi(i-1)},x_{\pi(i)})^2d\mathbf{x_{S_\pi}}}}=s.
The second inequality in Equation~\eqref{eq:approxexpect} follows from Equation~\eqref{eq:quickdecay} in a similar way.

issues.failure_explanation: At s = 1 (permitted since t < 1) the numerator and denominator of the displayed ratio are the same integral, so the hypothesis reads 1 = 1 + epsilon: the condition is satisfiable only with epsilon = 0, i.e. only by Kronecker-delta-type kernels, making the proposition vacuous exactly in the small-epsilon regime the framework needs; the paper's own Gaussian analysis yields only the limit R(s) -> s, not equality with s + epsilon for fixed epsilon > 0. Independently, the proof's final step for the upper bound of eq:approxexpect is merely asserted ('in a similar way'): under the natural one-sided reading R(s) <= s + epsilon, each B-side walk integral equals (E z^{l-1} + epsilon E z^l) times the corresponding A-side integral, and since E z^l / E z^{l-1} = (n-l)/(k-l) >= n/k under eq:specialdistrib, the walk sums give a ratio (k/n)(1 + epsilon (n-l)/(k-l)), which exceeds (1+epsilon)k/n for r >= 2; the two-sided conclusion does not follow from the hypothesis as stated.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the equality by a two-sided relative condition (e.g. |R_pi(s) - s| <= epsilon*s) required for all walk shapes and for all s = 1/z with z in the support of Xi; the proof's substitutions then give both inequalities of eq:approxexpect with the displayed constants.
issues.overall_effect: The paper's main quantitative theorem is vacuous as hypothesized and its upper bound is unestablished, so the claimed 1 +/- epsilon control of the expected normalized traces loses all content; the framework's theoretical guarantee (and, through it, the quantile-bound narrative) is unsupported.
issues.title: Quick-decay hypothesis (eq:quickdecay) forces epsilon = 0 and yields no upper bound
issues.why_classification: A contained reformulation of one displayed hypothesis (relative rather than additive-exact decay) plus routine epsilon-bookkeeping restores a recognizably comparable guarantee; no new construction or global architecture is required.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: &=\int_{\mathbb{R}^k}\int_{[0,1/z_1]^l}\prod_{i=1}^r\kappa(y_{\psi(i-1)},y_{\psi(i)})z_1^ld\mathbf{y_{S_\psi}}d\mathbf{z}\nonumber,
\frac{\int_{[0,s]^l}\prod_{i=1}^l\kappa(x_{\pi(i-1)},x_{\pi(i)})d\mathbf{x_\pi}}{\int_{[0,1]^l}\prod_{i=1}^l\kappa(x_{\pi(i-1)},x_{\pi(i)})d\mathbf{x_\pi}}=s+\epsilon,
The kernel matrices under consideration come from a kernel with quick decay away from the diagonal applied to uniformly-distributed sets of points in Euclidean space of any dimension.

issues.failure_explanation: The statement is made for points in R^d and prescribes y_j scaled by (1/z_j)^{1/d} per coordinate, i.e. a cube of volume 1/z_j and linear size z_j^{-1/d}; the density factor z per point used in the proof is consistent with this, but the support is then a d-dimensional cube of linear size z^{-1/d}, not [0, 1/z]. The proof nonetheless works entirely with scalar variables, integrates over [0, 1/z_1]^l with density z_1^l, and applies the decay condition - which compares integrals over boxes scaled by a linear factor s - at s = 1/z_1. For d > 1 the domain-restriction ratio scales like s^d (as the paper's own Gaussian limit computation shows for d = 1), so applying the condition at s = 1/z_1 is wrong, and the moment bookkeeping would require fractional moments E z^{l(1-1/d)} rather than the prescribed integer mixed moments of eq:specialdistrib. The conclusion eq:approxexpect is thus established only for d = 1, while the framework is advertised for uniform points in Euclidean space of any dimension and is demonstrated in dimensions 3 and 6.

failure_location.quote: Define $x_i\sim U[0,1]$ and $y_j\sim(1/z_j)^{1/d}U[0,1]$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ and $1\leq j\leq k$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must either restrict the proposition and the framework's guarantees to d = 1, excluding the advertised regime, or rework the scaling together with correspondingly modified moment conditions and a new existence argument for the sampling distribution.
issues.overall_effect: The main quantitative theorem provides no guarantee in the paper's headline setting (moderate or high dimension); the theoretical support for the multi-dimensional examples and for the proposed intrinsic-dimension application is lost.
issues.title: prop:momentmatch is proved only for scalar points; the stated (1/z)^{1/d} scaling is never used
issues.why_classification: Every source-supported resolution either excludes the advertised any-dimensional regime - a major advertised loss, since the framework's raison d'etre is the moderate/high-dimensional setting - or requires a new construction and proof of the sampling distribution; no contained repair is available.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: consider the space $V$ of square-integrable functions on the compact interval $[0,1]$ with respect to the Radon-Nikodym derivative $x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k+1}$

issues.failure_explanation: The chain claims (1/((k/n)*binom(n,k)))*mu_l = <v_i, v_j>_V for i + j = l. The left side equals (k-l-1)!(n-k)!/(n-l-1)!, but with the stated weight x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k+1} and v_i = sqrt(n-k)(1-x)^{-(i+1/2)} the inner product is (n-k)*Integral_0^1 x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k-l}dx = (n-k)! (k-l)!/(n-l)!, which differs by the non-unit factor (n-l)/(k-l) (e.g. n = 9, k = 3, l = 0 gives 1/28 versus 1/84). The displayed Gram-matrix representation of H_{k,n} and H'_{k,n}, on which the positive-definiteness argument solely rests, is therefore false as written.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Use the weight x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k} instead of x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k+1} (equivalently, shift the exponents of v_i and w_j); with that single correction both displayed inner-product identities hold exactly and the Stieltjes-moment argument goes through unchanged.
issues.overall_effect: The existence of the sampling distribution Xi (the 'preprocessing step' of the framework) is left unproven as written; the construction of the matrix B and the moments it is supposed to match lose their supporting proposition.
issues.title: Gram-identity computation in prop:distributionexistence is inconsistent by a factor (n-l)/(k-l)
issues.why_classification: A one-token correction to the weight restores every displayed identity; the existence conclusion and all downstream uses survive unchanged.
